questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of 128-bit shifts, wrap-around logic, and edge cases where n==0. Requires a clean, branch-minimal implementation without loops.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise rotation across 128 bits
- Handling edge cases safely (n==0, 128-n)
- Avoiding undefined shifts across boundary bits

## Code Example
```c
uint128 rotateLeft128(uint128 x, uint8 n) {
  n &= 127;
  if (n == 0) return x;
  return (x << n) | (x >> (128 - n));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt for a language without 128-bit integers?
- How would compiler optimizations affect this implementation in real code?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests low-level bit manipulation skills without branches, common in performance-critical code. It demonstrates proper masking, shifting, and word size preservation.

## Key Concepts
- Bit masking with 0x5555 (even positions) and 0xAAAA (odd positions)
- Left/right shifts combined with OR operation
- Branch-free operations on fixed-width integers

## Code Example
```c
uint16_t swapAdjacentBits16(uint16_t x) {
  return ((x & 0x5555) << 1) | ((x & 0xAAAA) >> 1);
}
```

## Examples
- Input: `0b10110011` (179) → Output: `0b01101101` (109)
- Input: `0b11110000` (240) → Output: `0b11110000` (240)

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This tests precise bit manipulation skills for rearranging 8-byte blocks without loops, essential for portable endianness handling in systems programming.

## Key Concepts

- Byte-level masking with 64-bit constants
- Multi-stage shuffles to minimize operations
- Endianness portability across platforms

## Code Example

```c
uint64_t bswap64(uint64_t x) {
  x = ((x & 0x00FF00FF00FF00FFULL) << 8) | ((x >> 8) & 0x00FF00FF00FF00FFULL);
  x = ((x & 0x0000FFFF0000FFFFULL) << 16) | ((x >> 16) & 0x0000FFFF0000FFFFULL);
  return (x << 32) | (x >> 32);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you verify correctness of this implementation?
- What are the trade-offs between this approach and using built-in byte swap functions?
- How would this differ on a little-endian vs big-endian system?
